text:
At even strength this was close to a draw. Minnesota and San Jose each created about a goal and a half of expected goals (the quality of their chances) with the teams at full strength, 1.47 for the Wild and 1.53 for the Sharks. The difference was what happened when somebody went to the box, and who was on the ice when it mattered.

Kirill Kaprizov opened it on the power play at 7:55 of the first, from Quinn Hughes and Matt Boldy. Macklin Celebrini, who played 25 minutes and put six shots on goal, tipped one in at 12:11 of the second to tie it and push San Jose's win chance from 27% to 48%. It didn't last. Maxim Shabanov tipped home a power-play goal at 14:15, with Kaprizov and Hughes on it again, and that goal moved Minnesota from 54% to 75%.

The Wild went 2 for 5 with the man advantage on 2.05 expected goals, which is a lot of good looks from five power plays. The Sharks went 0 for 3. In the third, Minnesota pulled away on chances as well, 1.46 to 0.36, and two shots that rarely go in did. Hughes scored on a 3% wrist shot at 6:54, and Zach Bogosian made it 4-1 at 13:58 on a slap shot given a 2% chance.

Kaprizov finished with a goal and three assists. Hughes had a goal and two assists in 31 minutes of ice time, which tells you how much Minnesota leaned on him. Boldy had seven shots and nothing to show for them. Jesper Wallstedt stopped 23 of 24, saving 1.1 goals more than his shots deserved, and Yaroslav Askarov was close to neutral at the other end despite the four goals, including a big stop on Kaprizov in the second.

That is three straight for the Wild. The Sharks are winless in four (0-4-0), and their best chance of the night, a 28% look for Ivar Stenberg in the first period, missed the net. On a night when the even-strength play was this even, a young team can't afford to give a top power play five chances.
headline: Kaprizov and Hughes power the Wild past San Jose
